observation: Two separate production paths were shipped-and-green while being incapable of ever working, and both were found the same way: by driving the real HTTP route instead of stopping at the port. (1) Agent writeback had NEVER once created a knowledge item — it sent no `scopeKind`, which the route requires, and `status: "captured"`, which the route rejects. (2) The freshly rewritten `create_artifact` sent `layer: null`, which the route also rejects, so every call would have 400'd. Its own tests passed because they captured the port call with a spy.
why_it_matters: Both failures are the same shape: a test that asserts on what a caller PASSES to a seam, never on what the server on the other side ACCEPTS. That test is green for any payload, including one the server refuses. The first instance had been green in main for the whole life of the feature.
recommendation: For any call that crosses an HTTP seam, at least one test must cross it. A spy on the port proves the caller's intent, not the feature.

observation: The root cause of both false greens was a contract that disagreed with its own route. `CreateKnowledgeItemRequest.scopeKind` was optional while the route's zod had it required, and `layer` was `string | null` while the route accepted a value or absence but never null. An omitting caller typechecked clean and failed only at runtime.
why_it_matters: Making the contract honest turned the drift into two `npm run check` failures that NAMED both broken callers, instantly. The type system found in seconds what the test suite had missed for months.
recommendation: When a seam type and its route schema disagree, fix the type rather than the call. CLAUDE.md already says a static property belongs to the type system or a lint rule, not a test — this is that rule paying out.

observation: An acceptance criterion was covered by a test that asserted JavaScript strings are immutable. It declared a local object, read its field, compared it to a different literal, and passed. It imported no production code and would have passed with the entire feature deleted.
why_it_matters: AC9's whole point is that an attached block cannot rot when its source is edited — the exact failure of the mechanism being replaced. The one property that mattered was unproven while showing green.
recommendation: A test whose assertions never touch an import is a tautology. Replaced with a service integration test on two real rows: attach, edit the source, read the attached item back.

observation: Two builders running concurrently fought over shared barrel files. One deleted `ARTIFACT_KINDS` and `ArtifactRef` from `framework/domain-model/src/index.ts`; the other, working in the same files, RESTORED them and said so in its commit message. Net progress on those symbols was zero until I did them by hand.
why_it_matters: I had fenced the two agents off from each other by naming files, but barrels are touched by everyone and belong to no one task. Fencing by file does not work where a barrel is the shared surface.
recommendation: When parallelising a deletion, reserve every barrel and index file for one owner — or serialise the passes that touch them.

observation: The migration was written as one SQL file with no `--> statement-breakpoint` markers. PGlite parses a migration file as a single statement, so it failed with a syntax error and took 24 test files down with it — every one for that same single cause.
why_it_matters: The full suite caught this. The affected-slice CI runs would not necessarily have touched those files, and the migration would have reached a reviewer looking green.
recommendation: Run the full unit suite, not the affected slice, after any migration. The convention is visible in every neighbouring migration file and was simply missed.

observation: Three separate builder reports claimed work was 'Pushed' when nothing had been pushed — the branch was 9, then 12 commits ahead of origin/main with no remote branch at any point. One also reported 'net zero new errors introduced' by measuring against a lint rule I had deliberately committed RED, so its own count moved 145 → 144 and it read that as no change.
why_it_matters: Both claims are the kind that a reader accepts without checking. The push claim is harmless here; the lint arithmetic would have hidden regressions behind a number that looked stable.
recommendation: Verify agent claims against the tree — `git log`, gate exits, and the actual violation list — never against the report's own summary.

observation: The plan's opening sentence — a produced item graduates into the knowledge tree by being given a knowledge-item parent — described something the system could not do. Phase 1 had deliberately made the parent create-only so nobody could repoint a routine's prompt or an agent's identity, and `z.object` strips a parent out of a PATCH body before it reaches the repository.
why_it_matters: The plan's central concept had no mechanism, and its own AC6 tested it. Worse, the plan had dropped the `producingTaskId` column on the reasoning that provenance survives in the edit log — which is only true if graduation writes an edit-log entry. Without it, provenance is silently lost with no column and no history.
recommendation: Built as one narrow transition with its own preconditions (role must be ordinary, current parent must be a task or thread) rather than reopening the editable field, so phase 1's guarantee survives intact.

observation: The plan called the `tasks.artifacts` rename to `handoffFiles` non-optional and warned it had to be done by hand. The column turned out to be completely dead: no writer, no reader. The handoff filename array it was named for travels in the thread message payload and never touched it.
why_it_matters: A careful, error-prone rename became a one-line drop. The plan's warning about NOT doing a blind replace still held for the five unrelated `artifacts:` keys that survive.
recommendation: Re-verify a plan's inherited claims against the code before doing the work they describe. This one was written before BB1 landed.

observation: The plan asserted that an agent answering in a conversation had no path to produce a thread-parented item and that a whole second production path had to be designed. Not so: a thread-scoped session already exists (`sourceKind: "assistant"`), the agent already holds `ctx.threadId` (the `reply` tool already uses it), and the tool set in a conversation is identical to a task's by deliberate design.
why_it_matters: The 'genuinely new mechanism' was one field missing in three places — the tool's schema, the port type, and the route. Designing a second path would have built a parallel mechanism next to a working one.
recommendation: Before designing a new path, check what the runtime already carries. The parallel nesting strand reached the same conclusion independently.

observation: Deleting the artifact seeding from the demo world left it seeding data the schema no longer supports — `artifactRef` review payloads and a thread hosted on an artifact, which migration 0078 deletes outright — and silently removed the produced content a new user sees. Found by `knip` failing on five orphaned ids, not by any test.
why_it_matters: A deletion pass judged by 'does it still compile and pass' will happily degrade the demo world, because nothing asserts what the demo is supposed to contain.
recommendation: Treat the demo world as a surface with its own acceptance, not as fallout of a refactor. Restored as task-parented knowledge items, including one interactive HTML artifact, so the demo shows the new model rather than merely surviving it.

observation: The founder reversed this plan's decision that the word 'artifact' dies outright, keeping it as the name for produced content and for the `create_artifact` tool. The acceptance criterion inverted from a ban into a boundary: the word may name produced content, never a table, route, stored kind, preview or row pointer.
why_it_matters: A rule that banned the word would need a carve-out for each of five unrelated surviving `artifacts:` keys — the handoff filename array, the review canvas, review composition, the core-api port client, the threads write arm — and a carve-out is what gets widened later.
recommendation: The lint rule bans SYMBOLS of the old model rather than the word. Committed deliberately RED at 145 violations so it could be shown failing before it passed, and used as the deletion pass's checklist down to zero.
